Consult Summary:
- Patient presents with two days of lower abdominal pain, mild nausea, increased urinary frequency, and low-grade subjective fever; possible urinary tract infection suspected, antibiotics prescribed.

History:
- Main complaint: Lower abdominal (lower tummy) pain for the past two days.
- Location: Central lower abdomen.
- Progression: New onset, no previous similar episodes.
- Associated symptoms: Feels hot and sweaty, mild nausea (no vomiting), increased urinary frequency, mild thirst, single episode of pinkish discoloration (blood) in urine.
- No current or recent fever above 37°C (measured once an hour ago at 37°C).
- Constipation last week, now resolved; normal bowel movement two hours prior to consult.
- No back pain, no strong-smelling urine.
- No abnormal vaginal discharge, no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.
- No shivering, no vomiting.
- No recent travel abroad.

Past Medical History:
- No significant medical history reported.
- Prior contraceptive implant (internal), used for one year, now discontinued (duration since removal not specified).
- Medication allergies: Amoxycillin.
- No current regular or over the counter medications.

Social History:
- Lives with parents.
- Does not smoke.
- Drinks alcohol: approximately four beers per week (one beer per occasion, four times a week).

Family History:
- Mother had breast cancer, diagnosed early and treated successfully.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Patient-reported temperature 37°C an hour before consult.
- No back pain or suprapubic tenderness reported; no positive examination findings (full exam not performed during teleconsultation).

Investigations:
- No investigations performed or recorded in this consult.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Suspected urinary tract infection (UTI)
  - Assessment based on lower abdominal pain, mild dysuria (increased frequency), mild hematuria (pink urine), subjective fever, and absence of red flags.
  - Plan: Prescribe a 3-day course of antibiotics (twice daily; specific agent and dose not documented).
  - Advise on warning signs (worsening pain, fever, new symptoms, back pain) requiring follow-up or face-to-face evaluation.
  - Start antibiotics as soon as received; obtain from allocated pharmacy.
- General advice:
  - Contact service immediately if symptoms worsen, recur, or new symptoms develop.

Quality checks (always include at bottom of note):

● Missing but clinically expected elements for a consult: 
   - Specific antibiotic prescribed, dose, route, frequency not documented.
   - No complete vital signs or abdominal examination findings recorded.
   - No medications reconciliation beyond allergies and prior contraceptive.
   - No urinalysis or laboratory investigations performed.
   - No detailed gynecological or sexual history.

● Internal conflicts from the transcript:
   - No internal conflicts noted.

● Brief comment on transcript quality if noisy/inaudible:
   - Some interruptions, unclear patient responses at times, but most clinical details adequate for telemedicine triage.
